title: Beef Tenderloin
description:
For special occasions, when you don’t want to go crazy with elaborate preparations, a beef tenderloin is the perfect choice. The meat is succulent, without fat (and almost good for you), and it’s relatively easy to plan for and prepare. What more could you ask for (except for making it a little cheaper, but what the heck, that’s what special occasions call for!)?
There are all kinds of approaches – pan searing, grilling, slow cooking, etc. – but this one seems the best. The technique is from Cook’s Illustrated, which is big on testing and specific techniques, but this one isn’t too technical and yields excellent results.
You can also “spice it up” a little by including some fresh rosemary sprigs under the shaping strings or making a little red-wine sauce to accompany the meat and maybe for some mashed potatoes.
Beef Tenderloin
Trim the fat and silverskin from the whole tenderloin (4-6 pounds) and choose the center-cut Chateaubriand (2 pounds), leaving the narrower tails for making petit filets or chunks for a quicker meal. (See next page for trimming instructions.)
Using 12-inch lengths of twine, tie roast crosswise at 1½-inch intervals. Sprinkle roast evenly with salt (2 teaspoons of kosher salt or 1 teaspoon of table salt), cover loosely with plastic wrap, and let stand at room temperature for 1 hour.
Meanwhile, adjust oven rack to middle position and heat oven to 300 degrees.
Pat roast dry with paper towels. Sprinkle roast evenly with pepper and spread unsalted butter evenly over surface.
ingredients: Transfer roast to wire rack set in rimmed baking sheet.
directions: Roast until instant-read thermometer inserted into center of roast registers 125 degrees for medium-rare, 40 to 55 minutes, flipping roast halfway through cooking.
Meanwhile, make a flavored butter from the next page.

Heat oil in 12-inch heavy-bottomed skillet over medium-high heat until just smoking. Place roast in skillet and sear until well browned on four sides, 1 to 2 minutes per side (total of 4 to 8 minutes).
Transfer roast to carving board and spread 2 tablespoons flavored butter evenly over top of roast; let rest 15 minutes.
Remove twine and cut meat crosswise into ½-inch-thick slices. Serve, with any of the extra flavored butter.

Cook the shallots, stirring occasionally, until the are soft and translucent, 10-12 minutes.
Turn the heat to high, add the wine and vinegar, and boil until reduced to a syrupy consistency (about ¼ cup), about 10 minutes.
Add the thyme and the beef broth and reduce to 1 cup, about 20 minutes.
Strain the sauce (it could be refrigerated overnight if you’d like).
Just before serving, reheat the sauce of medium heat. When it’s hot, whisk in the remaining 3 tablespoons butter.
Even though the whole beef tenderloin is an expensive cut, there is still some trimming to do to get the most tender Chateaubriand (about 2 pounds).
The starting piece will be about 4-6 pounds.
Locate the chain, the long piece of muscle the runs the length of the tenderloin.
Using you fingers, gently separate the chain from the tenderloin as much as possible.

With a boning knife, start at the narrow end of the chain and cut along the seam, making several long, shallow cuts rather than one or two deep ones. This way, you have more control over the path your knife takes and less chance of cutting in too far.
Starting about 1 inch from one end of the silverskin, push the tip of your knife under a strip of silverskin about ½ inch wide.
Using your free hand to hold the silverskin taut, angle the knife slightly up toward the silverskin as you slide the knife along the tenderloin, freeing the silverskin.
Then cut of the end of the silverskin that’s still attached. Repeat until all the silverskin is gone.
With the extra pieces, you can make some petite filets, or have little chunks for a stir fry, or use some of the fattier pieces for flavoring a sauce.
